A.explanation: Carrying 20 m horizontally at constant speed does no useful work on the sledge because there is no resultant force in the direction of motion and no gain in height.

B.explanation: Lifting needs work $W = mgh$ of about $50 \times 9.81 \times 1 \approx 490 \text{ J}$, which is much less than work against friction on snow.

C.explanation: With no friction on the ice, no sustained horizontal force is needed at constant speed, so work done on the sledge is essentially zero.

D.explanation: Pulling 10 m against 200 N friction needs $W = 200 \times 10 = 2000 \text{ J}$, larger than the lifting work of about $490 \text{ J}$.

hints: Notice the four different stages: 10 m with 200 N friction, 10 m with zero friction, a 1 m vertical lift of a 50 kg mass, and a 20 m horizontal carry at constant speed.
Recall that horizontal work is $W = Fd$ against the resistive force, while vertical lifting work is weight times height $W = mgh$.

Compare $200 \text{ N} \times 10 \text{ m}$ with $50 \text{ kg} \times 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2} \times 1 \text{ m}$, and ask how much force is needed to move at constant speed when friction is zero or motion is horizontal.
walkthrough: List the useful data: mass $m = 50 \text{ kg}$, snow pull $d = 10 \text{ m}$ with friction $F = 200 \text{ N}$, ice pull $d = 10 \text{ m}$ with $F = 0$, lift $h = 1 \text{ m}$, carry back horizontal at constant speed.
Use the work rule $W = Fd$ when force and displacement are in the same direction, and for lifting $W = mgh$ against weight $mg$.
For snow: the pull must overcome 200 N over 10 m, so $W = 200 \times 10 = 2000 \text{ J}$ done on the sledge.
For lifting: $W = mgh = 50 \times 9.81 \times 1 \approx 490 \text{ J}$ of gravitational potential energy gained.
For ice and for carrying back horizontally at constant speed: resultant horizontal force is zero, and horizontal carrying gives no height gain, so work done on the sledge is zero or negligible.
Compare $2000 \text{ J}$ with about $490 \text{ J}$ and zero: the snow pull is largest. This is option D
